The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states aiming to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

During the trial, Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals with Apple and partners to make Google the default search engine. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. Pichai stated the decision to pay for defaults was made with the consumer in mind, to gather data and be the best search engine across devices. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device to create inseparable services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software. In February, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours; Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed turning off history for a personnel matter unrelated to the hold. In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior; Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case is expected to continue for several weeks, potentially resulting in a Microsoft-like outcome where Google must change behavior, share APIs, and be banned from exclusive deals; Google might have to turn over collected data to other search engines, given the DOJ noted Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, with ripple effects on FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.

# See also

* [Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google over AI harms](../tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md) - Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, alleging violations of the Sherman Act and Clayton Act due to Google's anticompetitive use of publishers' content, readers, and ad revenue through technologies like Search Generative Experience (SGE), Bard, and the Knowledge Graph.
* [Apple defends Google Search deal in court: 'There wasn't a valid alternative'](apple-defends-google-search-deal-in-court-there-wasn-t-a.md) - Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google that Apple had no valid alternative to Google's search engine, negotiated the 2016 ISA with Sundar Pichai, and argued the deal prioritized user experience and privacy over economics.

Eddy Cue testified in the US v. Google antitrust trial defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA), which makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices. Although the ISA has existed since 2002, Cue negotiated the current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. During renegotiation, Apple sought a higher revenue share, while Pichai wanted to maintain the deal; they compromised on an undisclosed percentage.

Cue stated there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and that this remains true today. He argued the deal was driven by factors beyond economics, noting Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. Regarding user experience, Cue acknowledged the ISA did not allow Apple to offer search engine choice during setup, reasoning that showing engines users had not heard of would be detrimental. He further stated Apple makes Google the default because it is the best, while acknowledging users can easily change it, contrasting this with DuckDuckGo's CEO testimony that switching takes too many steps.

On privacy, Cue agreed Apple prioritizes user privacy and offers better protection than Google, citing ISA provisions requiring login-free searching and Apple's efforts to prevent tracking. When questioned about the ISA's impact on Apple's profits, Bellshaw suggested it might be significant, but Cue replied that Apple does not view it that way because the agreement succeeds due to the platform's overall appeal. Additionally, Google lawyer John Schmidtlein led Cue through Safari's history, highlighting seamless Google integration as a key user interface innovation mentioned in early promotional materials before 2003. Cue explained that pre-2003 users had to type specific URLs to search, whereas Apple introduced functionality allowing non-URL text in the URL field to trigger searches. Schmidtlein also argued Google helped Safari succeed by being a great product, referencing deals with Yahoo and Bing, and both men claimed switching search engines is easy and a non-issue.

* [Google antitrust case: key facts and trial developments](google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-trial-developments.md) - Overview of the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, including CEO testimony, financial data on default search engine deals, and potential regulatory outcomes.
